title: What is Missing from AI Post-Training AI: An Empirical Analysis
summary: The paper is a diagnostic analysis rather than a deployable method: it replaces the assumption that agent-run post-training pipelines improve strategy over time with evidence that agents lock into an initial strategy and only perform local adjustments, even with added experience scaffolds, human guidance, or inference compute. It costs nothing to adopt directly, but any team automating post-training with LLM agents must budget for human strategy oversight, since no tested intervention restored strategy-level revision. It can fail by being over-read as a solved problem: the scaffold gains are execution-level only, and the hardest tasks show almost no benefit from extra reasoning compute.
rationale: The work is a negative-result diagnosis of autonomous post-training agents, so the actionable takeaway is to keep human strategy review in any agent-driven training loop rather than to adopt a new technique.

claims.statement: The paper is a diagnostic analysis rather than a deployable method: it replaces the assumption that agent-run post-training pipelines improve strategy over time with evidence that agents lock into an initial strategy and only perform local adjustments, even with added experience scaffolds, human guidance, or inference compute. It costs nothing to adopt directly, but any team automating post-training with LLM agents must budget for human strategy oversight, since no tested intervention restored strategy-level revision. It can fail by being over-read as a solved problem: the scaffold gains are execution-level only, and the hardest tasks show almost no benefit from extra reasoning compute.

An experience-driven scaffold improves execution by +12.6 points on GSM8K and +40.8 on HumanEval, but leaves the agent's training strategy static; the paper quantifies no deployable end-to-end gain from fixing strategy lock-in.
